passage:
Salma, you think you notice everything? Let me tell you what happened to your Kiran Mama at ten. Our science sir wheeled a TV and a video player into class, a big event in our Bhopal school. On the screen, students in white and black shirts were passing a ball. "Count the passes by the white team," he said. I counted like my life depended on it. Fifteen! I was so proud.
Then sir asked, "Who saw the tiger?" Half the class laughed. I thought they were joking. He rewound it, and there it was: a person in a tiger costume strolling right through the middle, even waving. I had looked straight at that screen and never seen it.
Sir said, "You were looking, but your mind was busy counting." I've never forgotten that.

qa.q: How many passes did Kiran Mama count?
qa.a: Kiran Mama counted fifteen passes.

qa.q: Why did young Kiran think the class was joking about the tiger?
qa.a: Kiran was so absorbed in counting the passes, and so proud of getting fifteen, that the tiger never registered, and he felt certain there had been nothing to see.

qa.q: What lesson could Salma take from this story?
qa.a: Salma could remember that focusing hard on one thing can hide other things, so it helps to look again or check with others before being sure.

qa.q: What was it like for the classmates who spotted the tiger?
qa.a: They found it funny and were surprised others missed it, probably not realising they could miss things just as easily when focused.

grounding: It shows, through an uncle's memory, a child counting passes in a video who never sees a costumed tiger cross the screen.

passage:
The power had gone out in their Gangtok lane, and Pema's laptop was down to eight percent. "Quick, before it dies," Pema said. "The science club video. Count the passes by the red team."
Ira leaned in, a finger tapping each pass. Rain drummed on the tin roof. Pema held the torch, not counting, just watching.
"Eleven!" Ira shouted as the clip ended.
"Correct. And the panda?"
"What panda?"
Pema pressed replay with two percent left. A person in a panda suit walked slowly through the players, stopped in the middle, and beat its chest. Ira's mouth fell open. "That wasn't there!"
The screen went black. "It was," Pema said, laughing in the dark. "You just weren't looking for it."

qa.q: How many passes did Ira count?
qa.a: Ira counted eleven passes by the red team.

qa.q: Why was Ira so sure the panda "wasn't there"?
qa.a: Ira felt surprised, even shocked, because Ira's attention was fully on counting the red team's passes, so the panda never reached awareness and missing it felt like proof it wasn't there 🤔.

qa.q: What could Ira try the next time a video asks for careful counting?
qa.a: Watch once for the task and once more just looking at everything, since attention on one job can hide surprises.

qa.q: Why did Pema see the panda when Ira didn't?
qa.a: Pema was holding the torch and not counting, so Pema's attention was free to notice the panda walking through.

grounding: It shows a child counting passes in a video who misses a person in a panda suit, because attention, not the eyes alone, decides what is seen.

passage:
In Mrs. Pillai's Class 6 in Thane, the smart board showed two teams tossing a basketball. "Count the passes by the blue shirts," she said. "No talking."
Saurabh counted under his breath, fingers twitching with each pass. Chetan, beside him, was counting too, lips moving. The clip was only a minute long.
"Sixteen," Saurabh said. "Seventeen," said Chetan.
"Close," said Mrs. Pillai. "Now, who saw the gorilla?"
The room exploded. A few children waved their hands. Saurabh and Chetan looked at each other, baffled. She played it again, and a person in a gorilla suit strolled into the middle, thumped their chest, and walked off.
"No way," Saurabh whispered. "I was looking right there."
"That," said Mrs. Pillai, "is exactly the point."

qa.q: Whose passes were the children told to count?
qa.a: They were told to count the passes by the blue shirts.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's whisper "I was looking right there" show he felt?
qa.a: He felt amazed and a bit unsettled, realising that looking straight at something isn't the same as noticing it when attention is busy counting.

qa.q: How could Mrs. Pillai use this moment to help the class?
qa.a: She could explain that attention picks what we notice, and suggest pausing to look around when very focused, for example before crossing a road.

qa.q: What was it like for the children who did see the gorilla?
qa.a: They were excited and probably amused that others missed something so obvious, though they may have missed a pass or two themselves.

grounding: It shows children counting passes in a video who miss a person in a gorilla suit, showing that attention decides what is seen.

passage:
"Lokesh, count how many times the white team passes the ball. Ready?" Shankar Thatha held up his phone.
"Easy." Lokesh leaned in, lips moving. "...fourteen, fifteen, sixteen! Sixteen!"
"Correct. And did you see the bear?"
"What bear?"
"Watch again. Don't count this time."
Lokesh watched. Halfway through, a person in a big brown bear costume walked into the middle of the players, waved and walked out.
"No way! That wasn't there before!"
"Same video, kanna."
"But I was looking right at the screen!"
"Your eyes were. Your mind was busy counting passes. What the mind is busy with decides what you see."
"Play it again. I want to show Amma. She'll never spot it."

qa.q: How many passes did Lokesh count?
qa.a: Sixteen.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel on seeing the bear the second time, and why?
qa.a: Lokesh felt shocked and amazed, crying "No way!" because Lokesh had been looking right at the screen while counting passes and missed something that big.

qa.q: What did Shankar Thatha do that helped Lokesh understand, and why did it work?
qa.a: He played the same video again without the counting task, so Lokesh could see directly that attention, not the eyes alone, decided what was noticed.

qa.q: What might Shankar Thatha enjoy about watching Lokesh's reaction?
qa.a: He likely enjoys the surprise on Lokesh's face and the chance to teach something memorable without a lecture.

grounding: A child counting passes in a video completely misses a person in a bear costume, showing that attention decides what is seen.

passage: I'm Ankita, and last week I learned my eyes can fool me. In computer class, Jyoti Ma'am played a short video of children passing a football. "Count the passes by the yellow shirts," she said. I counted so hard my finger tapped the desk: twenty-two. I was right! Then Ma'am asked, "Who saw the tiger?" Half the class put up their hands. I laughed, because I thought they were joking. She played it again. A person in a big orange tiger suit walked slowly across the field, stopped, did a little dance and left. I felt my face go hot. How did I miss a dancing tiger? Ma'am said, "You were busy counting. Your mind chose." Now I try the same trick on Papa at home.

qa.q: How many passes did Ankita count?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: Why did Ankita's face go hot?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed and surprised after laughing at the others, and then seeing that a dancing tiger had been there all along.

qa.q: What could Ankita try the next time a task needs full attention but the whole scene matters too?
qa.a: Ankita could remember that focus hides other things and, after finishing, look again at the whole scene or ask what else was there.

qa.q: How might the classmates who saw the tiger feel when Ankita laughed?
qa.a: They might have felt a bit brushed off at first, then pleased when the replay proved them right.

grounding: A child counting passes misses a person in a tiger suit crossing the screen, learning that attention, not the eyes alone, decides what is seen.

passage: In the Class 6 science club, Rehana ma'am played a short video of students passing a basketball. "Count how many times the white-shirt team passes. Carefully." Gurleen leaned forward, lips moving. Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen. When the video ended, she shot up her hand. "Fifteen!" "Correct," said Rehana ma'am. "And did anyone see the tiger?" Half the room burst out laughing. Gurleen frowned. What tiger? Rehana ma'am played it again. Right in the middle, a person in a tiger costume walked slowly through the players, waved at the camera and walked off. Gurleen's jaw dropped. "That wasn't there!" "It was," said Rehana ma'am. "Your eyes saw it. Your attention didn't."

qa.q: How many passes did Gurleen count?
qa.a: Fifteen.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen insist 'That wasn't there!'?
qa.a: Gurleen felt shocked and puzzled, because her attention was so fixed on counting passes that the tiger never registered.

qa.q: What does this experiment teach Gurleen about noticing things?
qa.a: That attention decides what we see, so when focused on one task, it helps to look again or ask others what they noticed.

qa.q: How might the children who saw the tiger feel?
qa.a: They probably felt amused and a bit proud, laughing that anyone could miss something so strange.

grounding: Shows a child counting passes in a video and missing a person in a tiger costume walking through.

passage:
Monday. Bhavna didi showed Hrithik a video on her phone. "Count the passes by the red team." Hrithik counted eleven, proudly. "And the man with the umbrella?" There was no man. She replayed it. A man with a big black umbrella strolled right through the middle. Hrithik felt his ears go hot.
Wednesday. Hrithik made his own version with his cricket friends: count the catches, while Pintu walked through wearing a bucket on his head. He showed Bhavna didi. She missed the bucket. He laughed for ten minutes.
Saturday. He tested Papa at dinner. Papa missed the bucket too. "It's not your eyes," Hrithik explained grandly. "It's where your attention goes."

qa.q: What did the man in didi's video carry?
qa.a: A big black umbrella.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel on Monday when the video was replayed?
qa.a: Hrithik felt embarrassed, his ears going hot, having been so focused on counting that he missed something obvious.

qa.q: What did Hrithik learn by making his own video?
qa.a: That almost anyone misses something surprising when focused on one task, so it's about attention, not bad eyes.

qa.q: How might Bhavna didi have felt missing the bucket on Wednesday?
qa.a: Bhavna didi was probably surprised and amused, and understood how Hrithik had felt on Monday.

grounding: Shows a child counting passes and missing a man with an umbrella, then discovering that others miss obvious things too.

passage: Ayesha, you missed the bus because you were counting stickers? Sit with your Noor nani. When I was nine, in Rampur, my Abba made me count mangoes at his fruit stall every evening. One day a new crate came. "A hundred and twenty," he said. "Check it." I counted so hard my lips moved. Eighty-one, eighty-two. A goat wandered right up to the stall, stood beside me and ate three mangoes off the top of the crate. The whole bazaar was laughing. I didn't see it. I finished, proudly: "One hundred and seventeen, Abba! Three missing!" Abba laughed till he cried. My friend Shabnam from the next stall said the goat had even bumped my elbow. I didn't believe her until I saw the goat, still chewing.

qa.q: How many mangoes did young Noor count?
qa.a: One hundred and seventeen.

qa.q: Why didn't young Noor see the goat eating the mangoes?
qa.a: Noor felt so focused and proud about counting correctly that her attention shut out the goat, even though it was right beside her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nani's story, and what does it show?
qa.a: Seeing the goat still chewing, which showed that attention decides what we see, not the eyes alone.

qa.q: How did Abba react to Noor's report of three missing mangoes?
qa.a: Abba laughed till he cried, having watched the goat eat them right beside her.

grounding: Shows a child so focused on counting mangoes that she doesn't notice a goat eating them beside her.

The science club had only fifteen minutes before the bell, and the projector kept flickering. Ms Ankita played a short video of children passing a ball. "Count the passes by the team in white," she said.

Harish, eleven, leaned forward. One, two, three. The screen flickered. He kept counting hard. Eleven, twelve.

"Fourteen!" he called.

"Good. Did anyone see the man in the bear costume?"

Harish laughed. "What bear?"

She played it again. A man in a bear costume walked right through the middle, waved, and walked off.

Harish's jaw dropped. "That wasn't there!"

"It was," Ms Ankita said. "You were looking at the ball. Your eyes saw it, but your attention didn't."

qa.q: What did Ms Ankita ask the children to count?
qa.a: The passes by the team in white.

qa.q: Why did Harish say "That wasn't there!"?
qa.a: He felt shocked and a bit disbelieving, because he was so focused on counting that he truly didn't notice the bear.

qa.q: What lesson could Harish take from the video?
qa.a: When he focuses hard on one thing, he may miss others, so for important things he could check twice or ask others what they saw.

qa.q: How might Ms Ankita feel seeing the children's reactions?
qa.a: Ms Ankita probably feels pleased and amused that the experiment worked even with a flickering projector.

grounding: A child counting passes in a video doesn't notice a surprising figure crossing the screen, as attention decides what is seen.

passage:
On a Saturday in their Mumbai building, Tanvir and his neighbour Zainab were playing a game on the tablet: count how many times the cartoon frog jumped.

"Nine... ten... eleven," Tanvir whispered, eyes fixed.

Zainab's older brother, playing with them, asked, "Did you see the giant pineapple roll across the screen?"

"No way."

They watched again. A huge pineapple rolled slowly from left to right while the frog jumped.

"How did I miss that?" Tanvir said, amazed.

"You were busy with the frog," Zainab said.

Tanvir watched it three more times, giggling every time the pineapple appeared, as if it was new.

qa.q: What did the game ask Tanvir and Zainab to count?
qa.a: How many times the cartoon frog jumped.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir amazed when he watched again?
qa.a: He felt amazed and puzzled that he completely missed the giant pineapple while counting jumps.

qa.q: What could Tanvir remember the next time he's focused on something?
qa.a: Paying close attention to one thing can hide other things, so it helps to look around again.

qa.q: How might Zainab see Tanvir's surprise?
qa.a: Zainab seems amused and understanding, explaining he was busy with the frog.

grounding: A child counting jumps in a video misses a surprising object crossing the screen, as attention decides what is seen.

passage:
"Simran, count the bounces," said her uncle Vijay, pressing play on the video.

"Easy." Simran leaned close. "One, two, three..."

The ball bounced across a playground. Simran counted, lips moving.

"Twenty-one!"

"Right. And the clown?"

"What clown?"

"A clown walked past, juggling."

"No, he didn't."

Vijay rewound. A clown in a red wig strolled past, juggling three balls.

"But I was looking right at the screen!" Simran said.

"You were looking at the ball."

Simran thought. "So my eyes were there, but my brain wasn't?"

"Something like that."

"Play it again," she said, grinning. "I want to catch him this time."

qa.q: How many bounces did Simran count?
qa.a: Twenty-one.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when she saw the clown on the rewind?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a little indignant, since she was sure she had been looking at the screen.

qa.q: Which question helped Simran understand what happened?
qa.a: Her own question, whether her eyes were there but her brain wasn't, helped her see attention decides what she notices.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel watching Simran work it out?
qa.a: Vijay probably feels amused and pleased that she figured it out herself.

grounding: A child counting bounces in a video misses a juggling clown, showing attention decides what is seen.

passage:
In science week last winter, our teacher showed us a video of children passing a basketball. "Count the passes by the team in white," she said. I'm Avni, and I love counting, so I stared hard.
Fifteen passes. I was so proud.
Then Ma'am asked, "Who saw the bear?"
Half the class put up their hands, laughing. My friend Mahima said a person in a bear suit walked right through the middle and waved!
I didn't believe her. We watched it again. There it was: a big brown bear, waving at the camera for ages.
I felt so silly. But Ma'am said it wasn't about being silly. When your attention is busy counting, your eyes can look right at something and not see it.

qa.q: How many passes did Avni count?
qa.a: Avni counted fifteen passes.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when the bear appeared on the second watch?
qa.a: Avni felt silly and amazed, having looked right at the screen and still missed the bear.

qa.q: What did Ma'am explain, and how could Avni use it?
qa.a: That busy attention can miss something the eyes are looking at, so Avni can remember that focusing on one task can hide others.

qa.q: How did Mahima experience the video?
qa.a: Mahima noticed the bear and laughed, and had to convince Avni it was there.

grounding: Shows a child counting passes in a video who misses a bear crossing the screen, because attention decides what is seen.

passage:
Class 4 note, the week before Holi. Written by Bhavna, sports teacher.
At practice I asked the children to count how many times their partner bounced the ball. Parveen counted with total focus, lips moving.
Meanwhile the principal walked across the field carrying a huge tray of gujiyas for the Holi celebration and stood beside me for a whole minute. The children shrieked. Parveen didn't look up once. "Forty-two bounces!" she announced.
When I told her about the gujiyas, she stared at me. "The principal was here? Where?"
Her eyes were open. She just wasn't looking with her attention.
What I did next: I told the class that attention is like a torch; where you point it, you see. Then we all ate gujiyas, and Parveen got two.

qa.q: How many bounces did Parveen count?
qa.a: Parveen counted forty-two bounces.

qa.q: Why didn't Parveen notice the principal?
qa.a: Parveen felt determined and absorbed in counting, so her attention didn't take in the principal, even with her eyes open.

qa.q: What did Bhavna teach the class, and how could it help?
qa.a: That attention is like a torch, you see where you point it, which helps children understand why they miss obvious things.

qa.q: How did the other children react to the principal?
qa.a: The other children shrieked with excitement at the tray of gujiyas.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a child so busy counting bounces that she misses the principal carrying gujiyas across the field.

passage:
25 December, night.
Dear diary, today Jahnavi Didi came home from hostel with her hair cut really short. She sat next to me for an hour while I played my racing game, and I didn't notice. Not even when she said, "Notice anything?"
I said, "No, why?" without looking.
At dinner Mummy said, "Doesn't Didi look nice?" I looked up and nearly dropped my spoon. Her hair was gone!
Didi laughed so much. She said I had looked right at her three times.
I think my eyes saw her but my brain was in the race. Scary. What if I miss something important like that?
Tomorrow I'm going to play only after lunch, and look at people when they talk.
Saurabh

qa.q: What had changed about Jahnavi Didi?
qa.a: Jahnavi Didi came home with her hair cut really short.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel on noticing the haircut at dinner?
qa.a: Saurabh felt shocked and a bit scared, realising the eyes saw Didi but attention was in the race.

qa.q: What does Saurabh plan for tomorrow, and why does it help?
qa.a: Playing only after lunch and looking at people when they talk, so attention is free for what's around.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi Didi react?
qa.a: Jahnavi Didi laughed a lot, amused that Saurabh had looked right at her three times without noticing.

grounding: Shows a child absorbed in a game who looks right at a sister's new haircut and doesn't see it, because attention decides what is seen.

Mohit leaned in, lips moving. Nine, ten, eleven. He ignored the black shirts completely. Fifteen, sixteen.

Mohit's jaw dropped. "That was NOT there before!"
"It was," Mehak Didi said, smiling. "Your eyes saw it. Your attention was busy."

qa.q: Which players did Mehak Didi ask the club to watch?
qa.a: The players in white shirts.

qa.q: What does Mohit's "That was NOT there before!" suggest he felt?

qa.q: What could Mohit do when something important might be missed?
